articles.title: Is Topuria Too Small for Lightweight?
articles.description: Justin Gaethje believes Ilia Topuria belongs back at 145 pounds. Chael Sonnen's response? No. It's not that Topuria could never return to featherweight. Chael believes there's one thing that would have to happen first: Ilia would need to finish his business at lightweight and recapture the 155-pound title. Chael explains why fighters like Topuria don't change divisions to escape a problem, why moving back to featherweight now would go against the mentality that got Ilia this far, and what Alexander Volkanovski's pursuit of a second championship can teach us about the psychology of fighting with another belt still waiting at home. Could Topuria vs. Volkanovski happen again at 145? Chael loves the matchup. He just doesn't believe Ilia will entertain it until he has accomplished what he set out to do at lightweight. Will Gaethje Fight Again?
articles.description: Justin Gaethje says he's taking the rest of 2026 off to enjoy being champion, and that decision could completely change what his next fight looks like. Chael Sonnen breaks down Gaethje's comments on the lightweight division, including his belief that Ilia Topuria belongs back at featherweight and that Arman Tsarukyan could beat him. But there's another possibility: while Gaethje waits, the contenders beneath him may have to fight each other. Tsarukyan, Paddy Pimblett and Topuria could all have very different situations by the time Gaethje is ready to return. The opponent who makes the most sense today might not even be available when the UFC finally makes the call. Chael explains why Gaethje's decision to wait could put him in an unusually powerful position and why predicting his next opponent right now may be impossible. articles.title: Volkov is happy for "Mentally Ill" Josh Hokit
articles.description: Chael Sonnen has had a problem with Alexander Volkov for years, but it's actually a compliment. Volkov has done almost everything right. He's fought the best heavyweights in the world, stepped up as one of the UFC's earliest backup fighters, and Chael still believes Volkov beat Ciryl Gane despite losing the decision. The problem? He's never consistently demanded what he deserves. That may finally be changing. After seeing Volkov take aim at Josh Hokit and then digging through some of his older comments, Chael realized there's another side to Volkov that fans rarely get to see. He's funny, creative and understands how to get people talking. Now Chael wants him to take that personality away from social media and put it where it matters most: on the microphone. Josh Hokit has shown exactly how powerful that can be. Chael explains why Volkov should take notice and start playing the promotional game that could finally push him toward a UFC heavyweight title opportunity. articles.title: Jon Jones Deserves Some Credit #ufc
articles.description: Chael Sonnen was ready to go after Jon Jones—but then Jon said something that completely changed the conversation. Chael explains why he expected to criticize Jones, only to hear a statement he actually agreed with. Instead of dragging out a situation, Jon advocated for getting an injured fighter medical attention as quickly as possible rather than bringing him back into the center of the Octagon for an interview. Chael says that mindset reflects a different side of Jon Jones, arguing that Jones appears more mature and even more likable now than he was during his fighting career. The conversation also raises a bigger question about UFC post-fight interviews: when a fighter has just suffered a knockout or significant damage, should they really be brought back into the spotlight immediately? Chael breaks down why he believes Jon got this one right—and why that surprised him. #UFC #MMA #JonJones #ChaelSonnen #UFCNews #MMAFighters #UFCInterviews #JonJonesNews

articles.title: Did Ilia Just Accuse Gaethje of Cheating? #ufc
articles.description: Did Ilia Topuria just accuse Justin Gaethje of cheating? Chael Sonnen breaks down Ilia’s recent comments about Gaethje’s gloves and explains why he doesn’t necessarily interpret them as a serious accusation. According to Chael, Ilia may have been making a tongue-in-cheek comment about how hard Gaethje hits rather than claiming there was actually something illegal on or inside the glove. Either way, the comment has created exactly what a rematch needs: conversation. With Ilia Topuria and Justin Gaethje seemingly headed toward another fight, Chael explains why this unexpected back-and-forth could actually be useful for building interest in the matchup. articles.title: Jon Jones vs Daniel Cormier: The Brawl, The Hearing & The $50,000 Fine (12 Years Ago Today)
articles.description: Jon Jones vs Daniel Cormier: The Brawl, The Hearing & The $50,000 Fine (12 Years Ago Today) On September 23, 2014, the Nevada Athletic Commission ruled on the UFC 178 media-day brawl between Jon Jones and Daniel Cormier. Hours before the Aug. 4 face-off, Cormier told MMA Weekly he would "attack him the whole time." Then the two men touched foreheads on stage, Cormier shoved, Jones swung, and both went off the stage into the MGM Grand lobby. Eight days later Jones withdrew injured and UFC 178's main event collapsed — but Nevada still wanted answers. At the hearing, Jones told commissioners "I made us all look bad… as a man I sit here to accept them," and admitted the brawl cost him his Nike sponsorship. Cormier argued self-defense — "a reaction to him putting his head on mine" — and said he had no Nike deal to lose. The commission's ruling: no suspension for either man. Jones was fined $50,000 with 40 hours of community service; Cormier $9,000 with 20 hours. The motion passed unanimously. Outside the room, Cormier called it fair. They finally fought at UFC 182 on January 3, 2015. Jones won by unanimous decision. articles.title: Jon Jones Did the Right Thing
articles.description: I have spent years waiting for Jon Jones to give me a reason to bury him on camera, and the man keeps making it impossible. At UFC 331, Sean Sharaf knocked out Gable Steveson in twelve seconds, the third fastest heavyweight finish in UFC history. Before Bruce Buffer could even announce it, Jones pulled his fighter out of the cage and took him backstage. The Crypto.com Arena crowd booed. Gable caught all the heat. Then Jones stepped in front of it on X: it was my decision, the first time I'd ever been in that spot, and my only concern was getting my friend to the back to make sure he was okay. He praised Gable's work ethic, said he'll be back, and believes he'll be one of the best heavyweights in the UFC. I showed up ready to embarrass the whole lot of them, the retirement, the coaching gig at Real American Freestyle, all of it. Instead, I watched Jones turn out to be an excellent coach, saw the genuine bond he has with Gable, and watched him absorb the backlash his athlete would have taken. That's what a corner is supposed to do. A guy gets knocked out cold, you don't stand him up for a photo op, you get him to the back. Jones is sensitive to social media and knew he'd get roasted. He did it anyway. It pains me to say it, but Jon Jones was right. articles.title: What Is Ilia Saying About Gaethje's Gloves?
articles.description: Ilia Topuria finally broke his silence, and the internet decided to read him like a legal document. So let me do a little damage control, because I think I know what the man actually meant. Topuria lost to Justin Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 on the White House lawn, then said nothing for weeks. Nothing about moving to a new continent, building a brand-new gym, a year-plus layoff, or fighting five rounds against your favorite fighter's favorite fighter. The man had five verifiable excuses and never used a single one. Then he posted that next time he'd make sure they check Gaethje's gloves so nothing weird ends up on them, and everybody screamed accusation. Here's the thing. English is not his first language, and he said ON the glove, not IN the glove. Read it like a reasonable person and it's a compliment: man, Justin hits so hard I need to check those gloves. I took it the same way I took it in high school when a rival accused me of steroids because my chest looked strong. Andy Foster and the commission inspected everything. Nothing was there. And whether you take him literally or not, the whole saga gave this rematch the back-and-forth it was missing. So be a literalist if you want. Volkov has the ranking, the résumé and, in Chael's view, a legitimate argument that he already did enough against Gane to earn a championship opportunity. Pereira presents an entirely different challenge, and Volkov brings something particularly interesting against Alex: an experienced kickboxer who is considerably bigger than him. There's also Pereira's recent trip to the UFC offices. Chael doesn't believe fighters get brought in simply to hear ideas. He thinks something significant was finalized. Chael doesn't have an inside scoop on this one, but he's willing to make the call: Pereira vs. Volkov. articles.title: This Day in MMA: Jones vs. Gustafsson: The Night Toronto Booed the Decision | Sept. 21
articles.description: September 21, 2013 — Jon Jones and Alexander Gustafsson delivered one of the greatest championship fights in UFC history at UFC 165 in Toronto. Gustafsson became the first fighter to take Jones down and pushed the champion through five brutal rounds. Jones rallied with a pivotal spinning elbow in Round 4 and retained his title by unanimous decision: 48–47, 48–47 and 49–46. The Toronto crowd booed the decision. Jones left on a stretcher, and both fighters were taken to the hospital. The Fight of the Night classic entered the UFC Hall of Fame’s Fight Wing in 2021. This reel features Dana White discussing how close the doctor came to stopping the fight, Jones during the 2013 pre-fight call and both fighters after their 2018 rematch.
